Memory.value: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.
Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger
My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together

vignette:
Evan, a 29-year-old European American Coast Guard serviceman, came for help after months of feeling increasingly unsettled by an assault that had happened on an ordinary night off duty. He had been walking alone back to his apartment after meeting a friend for dinner, cutting through a downtown parking area he had used many times before. Two men stepped out from between parked cars, one demanding his wallet while the other moved in close enough that Evan could smell alcohol on his breath. The details he most readily recalled were not arranged like a story but surfaced as separate flashes: the glare of a security light on the pavement, the hard edge of a forearm across his chest, the sound of his own boots scraping backward against gravel, one man’s hand gripping his jacket pocket. He knew there had been a knife because he could remember seeing the flash of metal in one abrupt moment, but when he tried to describe the sequence to others, the event seemed to fall apart. He would start to tell it and then stop, saying that he could not seem to put it into words. Even now, when he could recall what happened, he often felt strangely numb, as if the whole scene belonged to somebody else and he were reporting on a stranger’s misfortune rather than his own.

In the weeks that followed, Evan found that the memory returned to him in disconnected pieces that did not fit together. He could remember the pavement under his shoes and then, without transition, the pressure of being shoved against a car door. He could recall the men’s faces in fragments, never as a complete image, and sometimes only the position of their hands or the shape of the knife in the light. At first he assumed he would be able to talk through it once the shock wore off, but when friends or his girlfriend asked what had happened, he gave short, careful answers and then changed the subject. He was embarrassed by how hard it was to explain something that had happened so quickly and so violently. In private, he tried to piece it together, but each attempt seemed to produce more gaps than clarity. He had come to believe that the memory itself had been broken by the event, leaving him with shards rather than a narrative.

Because Evan worked in the Coast Guard, the assault did not remain confined to memory in a simple way; it entered the daily environments where he moved through his shifts and his off-duty routines. When he was in uniform around docks, parking lots, or dim stretches of the base after dark, the same bodily sensations from that night could surface with no warning. A security light catching the metal on a tool cart, an unfamiliar man stepping too close in a lot, or the scrape of shoes on gravel could bring back one of those fragments, and for a moment he would feel stripped of context, as if the night had folded back on itself. He would go quiet, scanning the area in a way that was obvious to coworkers, then force himself to continue with his work. His relationship also began to narrow around the edges of the event. His girlfriend noticed that when she asked about the mugging, he would go still and say he did not know how to describe it. He was not refusing to talk out of indifference; rather, he seemed genuinely frustrated by the fact that the memory did not behave like a normal story and left him feeling blank in places where he expected emotion to be.

Over time, the sense of fragmentation became one of the most distressing parts of the assault for Evan. He kept returning to the same few pieces, hoping they would link together if he stared at them long enough, but they remained separate and oddly unreal. Sometimes he could recount the knife, the pressure at his chest, the shove, and then nothing, as though someone had cut out the middle of the scene. At other times, he could describe the entire incident in a flat voice and feel almost nothing while doing so, which frightened him in a different way. He worried that he was supposed to remember it as a coherent event and react with a clear emotional response, yet instead he found himself detached, unable to bridge the distance between what had happened and what he felt when he spoke about it. By the time he sought therapy, the assault had become something he could not properly narrate, something he kept trying and failing to assemble into order. What finally brought him in was the growing strain of living with a memory that would not settle into a story and would not stay comfortably in the past. He said he wanted to be able to talk about it without the words disappearing, and he was most afraid that, if it remained only as broken fragments and numb recall, it would keep intruding on his life in ways he could not explain to the people closest to him.
